draft.title: Volume of pyramids and cones
card: A pyramid has the same base and height as a prism. A cone has the same base and height as a cylinder. In each pair, the pointed solid holds one third of the volume of the other.
So for any pyramid or cone, \(V = \frac{1}{3}Ah\). Here \(A\) is the area of the base and \(h\) is the perpendicular height, from the base straight up to the tip.
For a cone the base is a circle, so \(A = \pi r^{2}\) and \(V = \frac{1}{3}\pi r^{2}h\). For a square pyramid with base side \(b\), \(A = b^{2}\).
A cone has radius 3 cm and height 4 cm. Then \(V = \frac{1}{3} \times \pi \times 3^{2} \times 4 = 12\pi\), which is about \(37.7 \text{ cm}^{3}\).
draft.remember: Pointed solid volume is one third of base area times height.

a.q: A square pyramid has base side 6 cm and perpendicular height 5 cm. What is its volume?
a.why: The base area is \(6^{2} = 36\), so \(V = \frac{1}{3} \times 36 \times 5 = 60\). The answer 180 forgets the one third, which only gives the volume of the prism.
a.clue: Find the base area first, then take one third of base area times height.

b.q: Leila's ice cream cone has radius 3 cm and perpendicular height 10 cm. What is the volume of the cone, to the nearest cubic centimetre?
b.why: \(V = \frac{1}{3} \times \pi \times 3^{2} \times 10 = 30\pi\), which is about 94. The answer 283 leaves out the one third. The answer 31 does not square the radius. The answer 377 uses the diameter 6 as the radius.
b.clue: The base is a circle, so square the radius before multiplying.

wants.brief: Two pairs of solids side by side: a square pyramid beside a square prism with the same base and height, and a cone beside a cylinder with the same base and height. Label the base "base" and the perpendicular height "h" on each solid, with a dashed vertical line for h inside the pyramid and the cone.
wants.why: Seeing the matching bases and heights shows what is being compared and where the perpendicular height is measured.
